title: The Good, The Bad And The Ugly For Eurozone Bonds
text:
The Good, The Bad And The Ugly For Eurozone Bonds

Cedric Gemehl

Gavekal Research | 27 Aug 2026

So far, 2026 has been a real rollercoaster year for Eurozone bond markets. As the start of the Iran war pushed energy prices higher, the yield on the BAML index of seven-to-10-year eurozone government bonds jumped from 2.87% on February 27 to 3.52% a month later. Then, as energy prices retreated, over the next three months yields fell back to 3.19% in late June. Since then, yields have climbed again, hitting 3.62% on August 24—above their March peak.This is significant. Yes, energy prices have also picked up since late June, once again pushing inflation expectations higher and leading markets to price in more European Central Bank rate hikes. But broadly, energy prices remain below their March highs (crude oil and diesel, for example, are down from March’s peaks, although wholesale prices for natural gas are up). In contrast, eurozone sovereign bond yields are now well above their March high. This suggests that there are other forces beyond energy prices driving up eurozone yields.
